title: After-storm checks on a smallholding
subtitle: A systematic walk-round to catch damage and welfare risks before the morning routine.
excerpt: A storm night on a smallholding can leave fence damage that lets livestock out onto roads, shelter roofs at dangerous angles, and water troughs contaminated by debris. A methodical walk-round at first light, done in a consistent order, means nothing gets missed. This guide gives a route and a checklist to follow after any storm of 50 mph or above.
sourceNotes: NFU, Farm Storm Damage Checklist (2023). Farm Safety Foundation, After a Storm: Guidance for Farmers (2022). Countryfile Magazine, Dealing with Storm Damage on a Smallholding (2021).

glossaryTerms.definition: Any section of fence, gate, or hedge that livestock could breach. After a storm, fallen trees, bent posts, and lifted rails all create new escape points.

content.text: The first priority after a severe storm is animal safety: are all animals present and where they should be? Carry out a headcount before anything else. Livestock that have escaped overnight may be on roads or in a neighbour's field. Contact the local police and any adjacent landowners immediately if you discover a shortfall.
Walk the full perimeter of every paddock that holds livestock, even if you heard nothing overnight.
Look for fallen trees or large branches on stock netting or wooden rails. A tree across a fence creates both an escape point and a potential entrapment.
Check all electric fence runs with a fence tester. Wet vegetation dragged across the tape by wind often grounds the fence without breaking it visibly.
Temporary repairs with stock netting and strainer posts: get the breach secure before attending to anything else. Use heavy staples or hinge-joint wire to close gaps rapidly.
Check all field shelters and open-sided buildings for structural movement. A shelter with a shifted roof line should be assessed for safety before animals re-enter.
Look for missing roof sheets, particularly on Dutch barns and polycarbonate-roofed shelters. Corrugated sheets become projectiles in storm-force wind and can carry several hundred metres.
Check stabling and housing for water ingress from lifted tiles or damaged fascia.
Check water troughs for debris. Leaves, branches, and dead animals fallen into open troughs during the storm require immediate cleaning before livestock drink.
If power is out, check whether electrically powered water systems (pumps, automatic drinkers) are functioning. Provide manual water if not.
Check fence energisers for damage, especially pole-mounted units.

If you find any downed overhead power cables, do not approach. Call Western Power Distribution (or your regional DNO) immediately, and keep livestock and people well clear. A fallen cable on a wet fence can electrify the entire run.

attrs.cue: Animals appear distressed or are grouping unusually after the storm
attrs.cause: Storm stress, a smell or noise stimulus still present, or one or more animals injured during the night
attrs.fix: Observe for physical injury: lameness, eye injuries, lacerations from debris. Calm the group by speaking quietly and moving slowly. Separate any visibly injured animal for closer examination.

attrs.cue: Large tree has fallen across a paddock and livestock may be trapped
attrs.cause: Storm damage to mature trees is unpredictable; older oaks and ash near paddocks are a known risk
attrs.fix: Approach slowly and check whether any animals are under or trapped by the tree before attempting to move them. Call a livestock vet or animal welfare officer if an animal is trapped and cannot be freed by hand.
